correctness.rationale: For every positive-definite quadratic form, sign-change averaging preserves the two-sided comparison with the Cesàro norm while removing the cross term, so diagonal quadratic forms suffice globally. For diagonal parameter \(t\), the squared distortion is the max/min ratio of \(F_t(s)=\sqrt{16+(1+s)^4}/(4(1+t s^2))\). At \(t=1/\sqrt{17}\), an exact factorization proves the endpoints are the only minima; derivative analysis proves a unique interior maximum at \(s_*\). Comparing that fixed interior slope with the appropriate endpoint shows every \(t\ne1/\sqrt{17}\) gives strictly larger distortion. The standard-library checker reproduces the root and decimals but is not used to justify global optimality.

originality.rationale: The 2006-online primary Cesàro paper defines \(\mathrm{ces}_p^{(n)}\), computes a James constant at \(p=2\), and explicitly leaves James constants at \(p\ne2\) open; its full text has no Banach--Mazur occurrence. The 2012 source treats only the Ptolemy constant of \(\mathrm{ces}_2^{(2)}\). The 2022 same-family paper treats a Gao-type constant, not affine Euclidean distortion. Targeted semantic and web searches using the object, invariant aliases, optimal ellipsoid language, and the characteristic \(\sqrt{17}\) parameter found no statement implying the exact \(p=4\) distance. The closest indexed results concern different bodies or different invariants.
residual_risks: A targeted literature search cannot prove global bibliographic novelty; an unindexed equivalent formula could exist.

The later same-family Gao-type article was only partially text-searchable during review, although the inspected Cesàro section concerns a different invariant and exact Banach--Mazur web searches returned no match.

value.rationale: Euclidean Banach--Mazur distance is a natural affine invariant of a finite-dimensional Banach space, and the two-dimensional Cesàro family is a classical object whose fine geometry has been studied through several exact constants. Exponent \(4\) is the first non-Hilbert even exponent after \(2\), so it is a natural benchmark rather than an arbitrary numerical slice: its squared radial profile becomes an explicitly tractable square root of a quartic while still requiring a nontrivial anisotropic optimizer. The result gives both the exact distortion and a global optimizer over all linear maps, and the symmetry-averaging reduction is reusable for other unconditional planar norms.
